{{Short description|Mathematical optimization method}}
The '''Barzilai–Borwein method'''<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1093/imanum/8.1.141 | title=Two-Point Step Size Gradient Methods | year=1988 | last1=Barzilai | first1=Jonathan | last2=Borwein | first2=Jonathan M. | journal=IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis | volume=8 | pages=141–148 }}</ref> is an iterative [[gradient descent|gradient descent method]] for unconstrained optimization using either of two step sizes derived from the linear trend of the most recent two iterates.  This method, and modifications, are globally convergent under mild conditions,<ref name=":1">{{cite journal | doi=10.1093/imanum/13.3.321 | title=On the Barzilai and Borwein choice of steplength for the gradient method | year=1993 | last1=Raydan | first1=Marcos | journal=IMA Journal of Numerical Analysis | volume=13 | issue=3 | pages=321–326 | hdl=1911/101676 | hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":2" /> and perform competitively with [[Conjugate gradient method|conjugate gradient]] methods for many problems.<ref name=":0">Fletcher, R. (2005). "On the Barzilai–Borwein Method". In Qi, L.; Teo, K.; Yang, X. (eds.). Optimization and Control with Applications. Applied Optimization. Vol. 96. Boston: Springer. pp. 235–256. ISBN 0-387-24254-6</ref>  Not depending on the objective itself, it can also solve some systems of linear and non-linear equations. 

== Method ==
To minimize a convex function <math>f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}</math> with gradient vector <math>g</math> at point <math>x</math>, let there be two prior iterates, <math>g_{k-1}(x_{k-1})</math> and <math>g_{k}(x_{k})</math>, in which <math>x_{k}=x_{k-1}-\alpha_{k-1} g_{k-1}</math> where <math>\alpha_{k-1}</math> is the previous iteration's step size (not necessarily a Barzilai–Borwein step size), and for brevity, let <math>\Delta x=x_k-x_{k-1}</math> and <math>\Delta g=g_k-g_{k-1}</math>.

A Barzilai–Borwein (BB) iteration is <math>x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha _kg_k</math> where the step size <math>\alpha _k</math> is either

:[long BB step] <math>\alpha _k^{LONG}=\frac{\Delta x\cdot\Delta x}{\Delta x\cdot\Delta g}</math>, or

:[short BB step] <math>\alpha _k^{SHORT}=\frac{\Delta x \cdot\Delta g}{\Delta g \cdot\Delta g}</math>.

Barzilai–Borwein also applies to systems of equations <math>g(x)=0</math> for <math>g:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n</math> in which the Jacobian of <math>g</math> is positive-definite in the symmetric part, that is, <math>\Delta x \cdot\Delta g</math> is necessarily positive.

== Derivation ==
Despite its simplicity and optimality properties, Cauchy's classical steepest-descent method<ref>A. Cauchy. Méthode générale pour la résolution des systèmes d’équations simultanées. C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris, 25:536–538, 1847.</ref> for unconstrained optimization often performs poorly.<ref>H. Akaike, On a successive transformation of probability distribution and its application to the analysis of the optimum gradient method, Ann. Inst. Statist. Math Tokyo, 11 (1959), pp. 1–17</ref>  This has motivated many to propose alternate search directions, such as the [[conjugate gradient method]]. [[Jonathan Barzilai]] and [[Jonathan Borwein]] instead proposed new step sizes for the gradient by approximating the [[quasi-Newton method]], creating a scalar approximation of the Hessian estimated from the finite differences between two evaluation points of the gradient, these being the most recent two iterates.

In a quasi-Newton iteration,

:<math>x_{k+1}=x_k-B^{-1}g(x_k)</math>

where <math>B</math> is some approximation of the Jacobian matrix of <math>g</math> (i.e. Hessian of the objective function) which satisfies the secant equation <math>B_k \Delta x_k = \Delta g_k</math>.  Barzilai and Borwein simplify <math>B</math> with a scalar <math>1/\alpha</math>, which usually cannot exactly satisfy the secant equation, but approximate it as <math>\frac{1}{\alpha}\Delta x\approx \Delta g</math>.  Approximations by two least-squares criteria are:

:[1]  Minimize <math> \|\Delta x/\alpha-\Delta g\|^2</math> with respect to <math>\alpha</math>, yielding the long BB step, or

:[2]  Minimize <math> \|\Delta x-\alpha\Delta g\|^2</math> with respect to <math>\alpha</math>, yielding the short BB step.

== Properties ==
In one dimension, both BB step sizes are equal and same as the classical [[secant method]].

The long BB step size is the same as a linearized Cauchy step, i.e. the first estimate using a secant-method for the line search (also, for [[Gradient descent#Solution of a linear system|linear problems]]).  The short BB step size is same as a linearized minimum-residual step.  BB applies the step sizes upon the forward direction vector for the next iterate, instead of the prior direction vector as if for another line-search step.

Barzilai and Borwein proved their method converges ''R''-superlinearly for quadratic minimization in two dimensions.  Raydan<ref name=":1" /> demonstrates convergence in general for quadratic problems.  Convergence is usually non-monotone, that is, neither the objective function nor the residual or gradient magnitude necessarily decrease with each iteration along a successful convergence toward the solution.

If <math>f</math> is a [[Quadratic programming|quadratic function]] with Hessian <math>A</math>, <math>1/\alpha^{LONG}</math> is the [[Rayleigh quotient]] of <math>A</math> by vector <math>\Delta x</math>, and <math>1/\alpha^{SHORT}</math> is the Rayleigh quotient of <math>A</math> by vector <math>\sqrt{A}\Delta x</math> (here taking <math>\sqrt A</math> as a solution to <math>(\sqrt{A})^T\sqrt{A}=A</math>, more at [[Definite matrix#Decomposition|Definite matrix]]).  

Fletcher<ref name=":0" /> compared its computational performance to conjugate gradient (CG) methods, finding CG tending faster for linear problems, but BB often faster for non-linear problems versus applicable CG-based methods.

BB has low storage requirements, suitable for large systems with millions of elements in <math> x</math>.

:<math> \frac{\alpha^{SHORT}}{\alpha^{LONG}}= \cos^2(\text{angle between }\Delta x\text{ and }\Delta g)</math>.

== Modifications and related methods ==
Since being demonstrated by Raydan,<ref name=":2">Raydan, M. The Barzilai and Borwein gradient method for the large scale unconstrained minimization problem. SIAM Journal of Optimization 7, pp 26-33. 1997</ref> BB is often applied with the non-monotone safeguarding strategy of Grippo, Lampariello, and Lucidi.<ref>L. Grippo, F. Lampariello, and S. Lucidi, “A nonmonotone line search technique for Newton’s method,” SIAM J. Numer. Anal., vol. 23, pp. 707–716, 1986</ref>  This tolerates some rise of the objective, but excessive rise initiates a [[backtracking line search]] using smaller step sizes, to assure global convergence.  Fletcher finds that allowing wider limits for non-monotonicity tend to result in more efficient convergence.<ref name=":0" />

Others have identified a step size being the [[geometric mean]] between the long and short BB step sizes, which exhibits similar properties.<ref>Varadhan R, Roland C (2008). Simple and Globally Convergent Methods for Accelerating the Convergence of Any EM Algorithm. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 35(2), 335-353.</ref><ref>Y. H. Dai, M. Al-Baali, and X. Yang, “A positive Barzilai-Borwein-like stepsize and an extension for symmetric linear systems,” in Numerical Analysis and Optimization. Cham, Switzerland: Springer, 2015, pp. 59-75.</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv | eprint=1812.02974 | last1=Dai | first1=Yu-Hong | last2=Huang | first2=Yakui | last3=Liu | first3=Xin-Wei | title=A family of spectral gradient methods for optimization | year=2018 | class=math.OC }}</ref><ref>Shuai Huang, Zhong Wan, A new nonmonotone spectral residual method for nonsmooth nonlinear equations, Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 313, pp 82-101, Elsevier, 2017</ref>
